ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a table with five columns, whose column headings are Round 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 in order. Below each column is given one match that the television station is to broadcast in that round: Round 1 is P–Q, Round 2 is R–S, Round 3 is P–T, Round 4 is T–U, and Round 5 is P–R. Reasoning: There are six teams P,Q,R,S,T,U. In each round, three matches are played simultaneously, so each round must divide the six teams into three pairs; and any two teams play each other only once. Team P is known to play Q in Round 1, T in Round 3, and R in Round 5, so P must also play S and U respectively in Rounds 2 and 4. In Round 2, S is already playing R, so P cannot play S and can only play U in Round 2. In Round 4, U is already playing T, so P can only play S in Round 4. Thus Round 2 has Q–T remaining, and Round 4 has Q–R remaining. Round 3 already has P–T, leaving Q,R,S,U. R cannot play Q, because Q–R is already in Round 4; R also cannot play S, because R–S is already in Round 2. So in Round 3, R must play U, leaving Q–S. Round 5 already has P–R, leaving Q,S,T,U, which at this point can be paired as Q–U and S–T. Finally, Round 1 already has P–Q, leaving R,S,T,U; among these teams, the matches not yet used and able to cover them in pairs are R–T and S–U. Therefore S plays U in Round 1.

raw_record.question_text: In a tournament each of the six teams plays one match against every other team. In each round of matches, three take place simultaneously. A TV station has already decided which match it will broadcast for each round, as shown in the diagram. In which round will team $\mathrm{S}$ play against team U?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a five-round table of televised matches: round 1 shows P–Q, round 2 shows R–S, round 3 shows P–T, round 4 shows T–U, and round 5 shows P–R. From the text, there are six teams P,Q,R,S,T,U; each round must contain three disjoint matches, and each pair of teams meets exactly once. Complete the schedule by forced placements. Team P already has Q in round 1, T in round 3, and R in round 5, so P must play S and U in rounds 2 and 4. Since S is already playing R in round 2, P must play U in round 2; since U is already playing T in round 4, P must play S in round 4. Thus the remaining pair in round 2 is Q–T, and the remaining pair in round 4 is Q–R. In round 3, after P–T, the remaining teams are Q,R,S,U; R cannot play Q because Q–R is round 4 and cannot play S because R–S is round 2, so R must play U, leaving Q–S. In round 5, after P–R, the remaining teams are Q,S,T,U; the only unused matching is Q–U and S–T. Therefore in round 1, after P–Q, the remaining four teams R,S,T,U must form R–T and S–U, so S plays U in round 1.

Image description: The figure shows a table with five columns, whose column headings are Round 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 in order. Below each column is given one match that the television station is to broadcast in that round: Round 1 is P–Q, Round 2 is R–S, Round 3 is P–T, Round 4 is T–U, and Round 5 is P–R.

Reasoning: There are six teams P,Q,R,S,T,U. In each round, three matches are played simultaneously, so each round must divide the six teams into three pairs; and any two teams play each other only once. Team P is known to play Q in Round 1, T in Round 3, and R in Round 5, so P must also play S and U respectively in Rounds 2 and 4. In Round 2, S is already playing R, so P cannot play S and can only play U in Round 2. In Round 4, U is already playing T, so P can only play S in Round 4. Thus Round 2 has Q–T remaining, and Round 4 has Q–R remaining.

Round 3 already has P–T, leaving Q,R,S,U. R cannot play Q, because Q–R is already in Round 4; R also cannot play S, because R–S is already in Round 2. So in Round 3, R must play U, leaving Q–S. Round 5 already has P–R, leaving Q,S,T,U, which at this point can be paired as Q–U and S–T. Finally, Round 1 already has P–Q, leaving R,S,T,U; among these teams, the matches not yet used and able to cover them in pairs are R–T and S–U. Therefore S plays U in Round 1.
